Over a **full** cycle a sinusoidal current spends equal time positive and negative, so
its average is **zero**.
**Step 1 — write the current.**
i = i₀ sin ωt ✓
**Step 2 — average it over one complete period.**
⟨i⟩ = (1/T)∫₀^T i₀ sin ωt dt
= **0** ✓
since the sine's positive half exactly cancels its negative half.
**Why the rms value is not zero.** The **square** is always positive ✓ so averaging i²
gives something finite:
I_rms = i₀/√2 = **6 A** here, as the question states.
**The half-cycle average, for contrast.** Over the **positive half** alone,
⟨i⟩_half = **2i₀/π = 0·637i₀** ✓
With i₀ = 6√2 = 8·49 A, that is **5·4 A** - a real quantity, and what a moving-coil
meter with a rectifier responds to. But over a whole cycle it averages to zero.
**Why rms is the useful measure.** It is the **equivalent d.c.** value ✓ the steady
current that would dissipate the same power in a resistor, since
P = I²_rms R ✓ The average current tells one nothing about heating.
**Why a d.c. ammeter reads zero on a.c.** Its moving coil responds to the **average**
torque ✓ which is zero for a sinusoid. A.c. meters therefore use rectifiers,
thermocouples or moving-iron movements, all of which respond to the magnitude.
**The peak value here.**
i₀ = I_rms√2 = 6 x 1·414 = **8·49 A** ✓
**Why the frequency is irrelevant.** The average over a **complete** cycle is zero for
any frequency ✓ The 50 Hz is given only to confirm that the current is alternating.
**What would make the average non-zero.** A **d.c. offset** ✓ A current
i = I_dc + i₀ sin ωt averages to I_dc - which is exactly how a rectifier circuit
delivers useful direct current.
**The physical meaning of a zero average.** Over each cycle, exactly as much charge
flows one way as the other ✓ so the **net charge transported** is zero - though energy
is certainly dissipated throughout.
**Reading the distractors.** **6√2** ✗ is the **peak** value. **6/(π√2)** ✗ and
**3/(π√2)** ✗ are related to the half-cycle average ✓ Only the full-cycle average is
exactly zero.
∴ Zero.

Find the **capacitive reactance**, then divide the rms voltage by it.
**Step 1 — read ω from the source equation.** From V = 50√2 sin 100t:
**ω = 100 rad s⁻¹** ✓
and the **peak** voltage is 50√2, so
V_rms = 50√2/√2 = **50 V** ✓
**Step 2 — find the reactance.**
X_C = 1/(ωC)
= 1/(100 x 10 x 10⁻⁶)
= 1/10⁻³
= **1000 Ω** ✓
**Step 3 — find the current.**
I_rms = V_rms/X_C
= 50/1000
= 0·05 A
= **50 mA** ✓
**Why the ammeter reads rms.** A.c. meters are calibrated in **rms** values ✓ so the
50 V rms, not the 70·7 V peak, is the figure to use. Using the peak would give
70·7 mA - which is the second distractor, and the designed trap.
**Why a capacitor passes a.c. at all.** No charge crosses the gap, but the plates
**charge and discharge** each cycle ✓ so current flows in the connecting wires. The
faster the alternation, the more current - which is why X_C falls with frequency.
**The frequency here.**
f = ω/2π = 100/6·283 = **15·9 Hz** ✓ a low frequency, which is why the reactance is as
high as a kilohm for so large a capacitor.
**How the reactance varies.**
X_C = 1/(2πfC) ✓
at 50 Hz the same capacitor would have X_C = **318 Ω** and pass **157 mA**
at d.c., f = 0, X_C = **∞** and no current flows at all ✓ which is why a capacitor
**blocks** d.c. while passing a.c.
**The phase relationship.** The current **leads** the voltage by **90°** ✓ and the
average power consumed is
P = V I cos 90° = **zero** ✓ The capacitor stores and returns energy each
quarter-cycle, dissipating nothing.
**The peak current.**
I₀ = 50 x √2/1000 = **70·7 mA** ✓ which is the second option - a correct quantity,
answering the wrong question.
**Reading the distractors.** **70·7 mA** ✗ is the peak current. **5·0 mA** ✗ and
**7·07 mA** ✗ are ten times too small, from mishandling the microfarad ✓
∴ 50 mA.

The inductive and capacitive voltages are in **antiphase**, so they subtract before
combining with V_R in quadrature.
**Step 1 — find the net reactive voltage.**
V_L − V_C = 40 − 120
= **−80 V** ✓ magnitude 80 V, the circuit being net **capacitive**.
**Step 2 — add V_R in quadrature.**
V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²)
= √(60² + 80²)
= √(3600 + 6400)
= √10000
= **100 V** ✓
**Why 3-4-5 appears again.** 60 and 80 are the legs of a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 20 ✓
so the hypotenuse is 100 - which is why examiners choose these numbers.
**Why the voltages do not simply add.** Each is a **phasor** ✓
V_R is **in phase** with the current
V_L **leads** it by 90°
V_C **lags** it by 90°
so V_L and V_C point in exactly opposite directions and 80 V of the 120 cancels.
**Why 220 V is the trap.** It is 40 + 120 + 60, the arithmetic sum ✗ which would be
right only if all three were in phase ✓
**The phase angle.**
tan φ = (V_L − V_C)/V_R = −80/60 = −1·333
**φ = −53·1°** ✓ the current **leads** the supply voltage, as it must in a net
capacitive circuit.
**The striking feature.** V_C = **120 V** exceeds the supply voltage of 100 V ✓
Entirely normal in a series LCR circuit, and near resonance the reactive voltages can
be many times the source - which is why such components must be rated carefully.
**What resonance would require.** V_L = V_C ✓ Here they are far apart, so the circuit
is well off resonance. Lowering the frequency would reduce X_C and raise X_L, moving it
towards resonance.
**The power factor.**
cos φ = V_R/V = 60/100 = **0·6** ✓ so only 60% of the apparent power is consumed.
**Reading the distractors.** **220 V** ✗ is the scalar sum. **160 V** ✗ is 100 + 60,
and **180 V** ✗ is 120 + 60 ✓ Only the quadrature combination gives 100 V.
∴ 100 V.

**Ultraviolet** radiation is used to sterilise milk and water - it destroys
micro-organisms without heating.
**Step 1 — see why UV works.** Wavelengths around **250-260 nm** are strongly absorbed
by **DNA** ✓ The absorbed photons, of about 5 eV, break bonds and form thymine dimers,
which prevent the organism from replicating. It is killed without the liquid being
heated.
**Step 2 — see why it suits milk.** The treatment is **cold** ✓ so the flavour,
vitamins and proteins survive far better than under pasteurisation at 72 °C. No
chemicals are added and no residue is left.
**Step 3 — note its one limitation.** UV has very little **penetrating power** ✓ so
the liquid must be passed in a **thin film** past the lamp. It sterilises the surface
and the thin layer only.
**Why the other radiations are unsuitable.**
**X-rays** ✗ and **gamma rays** ✗ would work - they are **ionising** and lethal to
microbes - but they are hazardous to operate, require heavy shielding, and can produce
chemical changes in the food. Gamma irradiation **is** used for some packaged foods,
but not routinely for milk, and it is not what the question intends by a simple
sterilising lamp.
**radiowaves** ✗ carry far too little energy per photon - about 10⁻⁶ eV - to damage
anything ✓ They merely heat, and then only by absorption.
**The photon energies compared.**
radio: **10⁻⁶ eV** ✗ harmless
visible: 2-3 eV ✗ too weak to break DNA bonds
**UV at 254 nm: 4·9 eV** ✓ just enough
X-ray: **10⁴ eV** - far more than needed, and dangerous ✓
**Where UV sterilisation is used.** Drinking-water treatment, hospital air and surface
disinfection, laboratory safety cabinets, and the sterilisation of packaging ✓ A
low-pressure mercury lamp emitting at 254 nm is the standard source.
**Why UV is dangerous to us too.** The same mechanism damages skin and eye cells ✓ UV-C
lamps must be shielded, and it is why sunburn and skin cancer follow UV exposure.
**The natural case.** Sunlight's UV sterilises surfaces outdoors ✓ which is why clothes
dried in the sun smell fresh and why the ozone layer, which absorbs most solar UV-C, is
essential to life.
∴ UV rays.

The apparent rise is **t(1 − 1/n)**, so the colour with the **largest n** rises most -
**violet**.
**Step 1 — write the normal shift.** For a plate of thickness t viewed normally, an
object beneath appears raised by
shift = **t(1 − 1/n)** ✓
**Step 2 — see how it varies with n.** As n grows, 1/n shrinks and the bracket
**grows** ✓ so a larger refractive index gives a greater apparent rise.
**Step 3 — rank the colours.** In glass the index is largest at the **violet** end:
violet > green > yellow > red ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** The **violet** letter appears raised the most ✓
**The numbers, for crown glass.**
violet: n = **1·53** → shift = 0·346t ✓
green: 1·52 → 0·342t
yellow: 1·517 → 0·341t
red: **1·51** → 0·338t ✓
A small spread, but a definite ordering - and the violet letter is raised about 2% more
than the red.
**Why violet has the largest index.** **Dispersion** ✓ The index rises as the
wavelength falls, following Cauchy's relation
n = A + B/λ² ✓
Violet, with the shortest wavelength, is the most strongly refracted - which is why it
is bent most by a prism and appears at the bottom of a spectrum.
**Why the letters appear raised at all.** Light from them bends **away from the
normal** on leaving the glass ✓ so the emerging rays seem to come from a point nearer
the top surface. The plate makes everything beneath it look closer.
**The apparent depth, as the other side of the same coin.**
apparent depth = **t/n** ✓
so the violet letter appears **shallowest** - which is the same statement as rising
most.
**Why the effect is small but visible.** The index differences are in the third decimal
place ✓ Over a thick plate the colour fringing becomes noticeable, and it is the origin
of the coloured edges seen through a thick glass block.
**A caution about the viewing angle.** The formula holds for **near-normal** viewing ✓
Looking obliquely gives a larger displacement and visible lateral colour separation.
**Reading the distractors.** **Red** ✗ has the **smallest** index and rises least - the
exact opposite. **Yellow** and **green** ✗ lie between ✓
∴ Violet.

If the emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident one, the first and last media must
have the **same** refractive index.
**Step 1 — apply Snell's law at each parallel interface.**
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ = n₃ sin θ₃ = n₄ sin θ₄ ✓
The product **n sin θ** is the same in every layer - the invariant of a stack of
parallel surfaces.
**Step 2 — impose the parallelism.** If DE is parallel to AB, the final angle equals
the initial one:
**θ₄ = θ₁** ✓
**Step 3 — combine.**
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₄ sin θ₄ = n₄ sin θ₁ ✓
so
**n₁ = n₄** ✓
**Why only the first and last matter.** The intermediate layers **cancel** from the
chain ✓ Each bends the ray one way on entry and the opposite way on exit; what survives
is determined solely by the media at the two ends.
**The familiar special case.** A **glass slab** in air: n₁ = n₄ = 1 ✓ so the emergent
ray is parallel to the incident one, merely **displaced sideways** by the lateral
shift. The slab in this question behaves the same way, however many layers it has.
**What the intermediate indices do control.** The **path** inside and the total
**lateral displacement** ✓ but not the final direction.
**Why n₂ and n₃ are unconstrained.** They may be anything, in any order ✓ The ray
zig-zags more or less steeply through them, but emerges parallel regardless.
**A worked check.** Take n₁ = 1, θ₁ = 45°, so n sin θ = 0·707 throughout:
n₂ = 1·5: θ₂ = **28·1°**
n₃ = 1·2: θ₃ = **36·1°**
n₄ = 1: θ₄ = **45°** ✓ exactly the incident angle.
**What the figure shows.** The ray bends progressively **towards** the normal at each
interface, and the labelled angles increase outward ✓ consistent with n increasing
then decreasing back to n₁.
**Where this principle is used.** **Graded-index optical fibres**, where the index
varies continuously ✓ and the **mirage**, where layers of air of differing density bend
light gradually. Both are limits of the same stacked-layer argument.
**Reading the distractors.** **n₂ = n₄** ✗ and **n₁ = n₃** ✗ constrain the wrong pair.
The **averaging** option ✗ invents a relation that no application of Snell's law
produces ✓
∴ n₁ = n₄.

Red and blue light have **different frequencies**, so the two beams are **incoherent**
and no interference occurs.
**Step 1 — recall the condition for interference.** The two sources must be
**coherent** - maintaining a **constant phase difference** ✓ which requires, above
all, the **same frequency**.
**Step 2 — see what the filters do.** One slit now passes only **red**, the other only
**blue** ✓ The two beams differ in frequency by nearly a factor of two.
**Step 3 — see the consequence.** The phase difference between them changes
**continuously and rapidly** ✓ Any fringe pattern would sweep past far faster than the
eye or any detector could follow, and the observed intensity is simply the **sum** of
the two.
**Step 4 — conclude.** **No interference** ✓
**How fast the phase runs.** The beat frequency between red (4·3 x 10¹⁴ Hz) and blue
(6·7 x 10¹⁴ Hz) is about **2·4 x 10¹⁴ Hz** ✓ The pattern would shift completely in
10⁻¹⁵ s - utterly unobservable.
**Why Young's original experiment worked.** He derived **both** beams from a
**single** source ✓ so any phase fluctuation affected both equally and the difference
stayed constant. That is the whole art of producing coherent beams.
**Why two independent lamps show no fringes either.** Each atom radiates
independently, in bursts of about 10⁻⁸ s ✓ so the relative phase of two lamps changes
randomly a hundred million times a second.
**What a laser changes.** Its light is coherent over metres or kilometres ✓ Two
**separate** lasers of the same frequency can be made to interfere - something quite
impossible with thermal sources.
**What would be seen on the screen.** Uniform illumination, the simple **sum** of a red
patch and a blue patch - appearing **magenta** where they overlap ✓ with no fringes at
all.
**What white light alone would give.** Coloured fringes, with a **white** central
maximum ✓ since all colours have zero path difference there, and increasingly coloured
and washed-out fringes further out.
**The three requirements for sustained interference.**
same **frequency** ✓
constant **phase relationship** ✓
comparable **amplitudes**, for good contrast ✓
The filters destroy the first, and with it the second.
**Reading the distractors.** All three fringe options ✗ presume a pattern forms ✓ The
difference in frequency forbids it outright.
∴ No interference.

The central maximum of a single slit spans **2λ/a** in angle.
**Step 1 — locate the first minimum.** For a single slit of width a,
a sin θ = λ ✓
so for small angles
θ = **λ/a** on each side of the centre.
**Step 2 — find the full angular width.** Minimum to minimum is **twice** that:
2θ = **2λ/a** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
2θ = 2(600 x 10⁻⁹)/(0·2 x 10⁻³)
= 1·2 x 10⁻⁶/(2 x 10⁻⁴) ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
= **6 x 10⁻³ rad** ✓
**Why the central maximum is twice as wide as the others.** It spans from the first
minimum on one side to the first on the other ✓ while each secondary maximum occupies
only the interval between consecutive minima, λ/a. The central fringe is therefore
twice as broad and far brighter.
**The intensity distribution.** About **84%** of the light falls in the central
maximum ✓ with the first secondary maximum carrying only 4·7% - which is why a single
slit produces one bright band with faint wings.
**Why a narrower slit spreads the light more.** θ ∝ **1/a** ✓ Narrowing the slit widens
the pattern - the counter-intuitive hallmark of diffraction, and a direct consequence
of the uncertainty principle applied to the photon's transverse momentum.
**The linear width on a screen.** At distance D,
width = **2λD/a** ✓ For D = 1 m that is 6 mm - easily visible.
**When ray optics takes over.** If the slit is much wider than the wavelength, θ
becomes negligible and the light travels in straight lines ✓ Here λ/a = 3 x 10⁻³, small
but measurable - diffraction is just becoming apparent.
**The contrast with the double slit.** There the fringes are equally spaced with
separation λD/d ✓ and the single-slit pattern forms an **envelope** modulating their
brightness.
**Why "measured from minimum to minimum" is stated.** Some texts quote the
**half**-width, λ/a ✓ The question removes the ambiguity, and the factor of 2 is the
whole difficulty.
**Reading the distractors.** **4 x 10⁻³**, **2·4 x 10⁻³** and **4·5 x 10⁻³ rad** ✗
correspond to no simple multiple of λ/a = 3 x 10⁻³ ✓ The answer must be exactly twice
that.
∴ 6 × 10⁻³ rad.

The **Fresnel distance** z = a²/λ marks where diffraction begins to matter.
**Step 1 — state the criterion.** A beam of aperture a travels in a nearly straight
line out to
z_F = **a²/λ** ✓
beyond which its diffractive spreading becomes comparable with the aperture itself.
**Step 2 — substitute.**
z_F = (4 x 10⁻³)²/(400 x 10⁻⁹)
= 1·6 x 10⁻⁵/(4 x 10⁻⁷) ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
= **40 m** ✓
**Where the criterion comes from.** The beam spreads through an angle θ ≈ λ/a ✓ so
after a distance z the spreading is zθ = zλ/a. Setting that equal to the aperture a
gives z = **a²/λ** - the distance at which diffraction has doubled the beam's width.
**What it means in practice.** For z ≪ z_F, **ray optics** is an excellent
approximation ✓ beyond it, the wave nature dominates and the beam fans out.
**Why the criterion is so useful.** It tells one when the simple rules of geometrical
optics may be trusted ✓ Shadows are sharp within the Fresnel distance and blur beyond
it.
**How it scales.** z_F ∝ **a²** ✓ so doubling the aperture **quadruples** the usable
distance. An 8 mm aperture would give 160 m.
**A worked comparison for a laser.** A 2 mm beam of 633 nm light:
z_F = (2 x 10⁻³)²/(6·33 x 10⁻⁷) = **6·3 m** ✓ which is why a laser pointer's spot stays
tight across a room but spreads noticeably across a field.
**Why telescopes and microscopes need large apertures.** The resolving angle is
**1·22λ/a** ✓ so a bigger aperture resolves finer detail - the same 1/a that governs
the Fresnel distance.
**The two regimes named.**
**Fresnel** (near-field) diffraction: z comparable with z_F ✓
**Fraunhofer** (far-field) diffraction: z ≫ z_F ✓ which is the regime of the standard
single-slit and grating formulas.
**A sanity check.** 40 m is a plausible distance for a 4 mm beam ✓ Light through a
window of 1 m aperture would travel 2500 km before diffracting appreciably - which is
why shadows in daily life are sharp.
**Reading the distractors.** **24 m**, **18 m** and **30 m** ✗ correspond to no
combination of a² and λ ✓ The arithmetic 1·6 x 10⁻⁵ ÷ 4 x 10⁻⁷ = 40 settles it.
∴ 40 m.

Use the standard shortcut **λ = 12·27/√V Å**.
**Step 1 — recall the relation.** An electron accelerated through V volts has
λ = h/√(2meV) = **12·27/√V Å** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute V = 400.**
√400 = **20** ✓
λ = 12·27/20
= **0·61 Å** ✓
**Step 3 — convert to nanometres.**
0·61 Å = 0·061 nm
≈ **0·06 nm** ✓
**The derivation, for completeness.**
p = √(2meV) = √(2 x 9·1 x 10⁻³¹ x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ x 400) = **1·08 x 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹**
λ = h/p = 6·63 x 10⁻³⁴/1·08 x 10⁻²³ = **6·1 x 10⁻¹¹ m** ✓ the same.
**Why this wavelength is so useful.** 0·06 nm is comparable with **atomic spacings**,
a few tenths of a nanometre ✓ which is why electrons of this energy diffract from
crystals - the Davisson-Germer experiment, and the basis of electron diffraction as a
structural tool.
**Comparison with light.** Visible light has λ ≈ **500 nm**, some **8000 times**
longer ✓ Since resolution is limited by wavelength, an electron microscope sees detail
thousands of times finer than any optical one.
**How the wavelength scales.** λ ∝ **1/√V** ✓
100 V: **0·123 nm**
400 V: **0·061 nm** ✓
10 kV: **0·0123 nm**
Quadrupling the voltage halves the wavelength.
**Why electron microscopes run at tens of kilovolts.** To push λ down to picometres ✓
In practice lens aberrations, not the wavelength, limit the resolution to about 0·05 nm.
**The relativistic caveat.** Above about 50 kV the formula overestimates λ ✓ At 400 V
the electron's speed is 1·2 x 10⁷ m s⁻¹, only 4% of c, so the correction is negligible.
**The electron's speed here.**
v = √(2eV/m) = **1·19 x 10⁷ m s⁻¹** ✓
**Why de Broglie's idea was so bold.** He proposed in 1924 that **matter** has a
wavelength, by analogy with light's particle nature ✓ Three years later electron
diffraction confirmed it, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1929.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·03 nm** ✗ corresponds to 1600 V. **0·04 nm** ✗ to
900 V, and **0·12 nm** ✗ to 100 V ✓ The 1/√V dependence makes each a different
accelerating voltage.
∴ 0.06 nm.
